{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_d333ed964b7c4ac1bc8be054","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Decisions & rationale\n2\t\n3\t## Naming\n4\t\n5\t**Trail Boss** — on a cattle drive, the trail boss is in overall command: sets the direction,\n6\tmakes the calls, and rides in when a steer bogs down or strays. The product runs a *herd* of\n7\tagent sessions; when one gets stuck it reports in, and you — the trail boss — ride over and set\n8\tit right. The metaphor maps cleanly onto the mechanism:\n9\t\n10\t- **the herd grazing the range** → sessions working autonomously\n11\t- **a steer bogs down or strays** → a `Stop` / `PermissionRequest` hook fires; the collector\n12\t  flags the session stuck\n13\t- **the trail boss rides over and sets it right** → you read the context and give the order\n14\t  (reply) or wave it on (skip); the queue surfaces stuck sessions oldest-first (flat FIFO, no\n15\t  priority ranking)\n16\t\n17\t### Names considered and rejected\n18\t\n19\t- **`agent-inbox`** — clearest literal description, but collides head-on with\n20\t  [`langchain-ai/agent-inbox`](https://github.com/langchain-ai/agent-inbox), an existing\n21\t  human-in-the-loop inbox for LangGraph agents. Would read as derivative and lose every search.\n22\t- **`agent-attention`** — names the value prop (your attention is the scarce resource being\n23\t  routed), but risks reading as the ML \"attention\" mechanism.\n24\t- **`agent-central`** — self-explanatory but generic, and \"central\" reads like a passive\n25\t  dashboard/hub rather than an act-on-the-stuck-one tool.\n26\t\n27\tTrail Boss keeps a memorable, distinctive identity; the tagline carries the legibility for\n28\tnewcomers.\n29\t\n30\t## Design decisions\n31\t\n32\t### Normalized event API endpoint (2026-07-02)\n33\t\n34\t**Decision:** Add a dedicated `/event/normalized` endpoint that accepts pre-normalized stuck/unstuck events.\n35\t\n36\t**Rationale:**\n37\t\n38\tThe daemon architecture separates detection (harness-coupled) from the core queue logic (harness-agnostic). To maintain this separation, we need a normalized event contract that isolates harness coupling to the adapter layer.\n39\t\n40\tTwo approaches were considered:\n41\t\n42\t1. **New normalized endpoint** (`/event/normalized`): Accepts pre-normalized events with a `type` field. Harness-specific adapters (Claude Code hooks, tmux detector) emit normalized events directly.\n43\t2. **Server-side adapter wrapper**: Keep single `/event` endpoint, register multiple server-side adapters that wrap different event formats in a common Claude hook format.\n44\t\n45\t**Option 1 was chosen** for these reasons:\n46\t\n47\t- **Clean separation**: The adapter lives at the emission site (hook script or detector), not in the daemon. The daemon consumes only normalized events and has no knowledge of harness-specific formats.\n48\t- **Protocol simplicity**: A single `type` field enables discriminated unions and type guards. No header-based routing or format detection required.\n49\t- **Extensibility**: Adding a new harness means writing a new emitter/adapter that outputs normalized events; the daemon remains unchanged.\n50\t- **Testability**: Synthetic events can be POSTed directly to `/event/normalized` without constructing hook payloads.\n51\t\n52\t**Event schema:**\n53\t\n54\tAll normalized events share a common structure with a `type` discriminator:\n55\t\n56\t```typescript\n57\t// StuckEvent — session became stuck and needs attention\n58\t{\n59\t  type: \"stuck\"\n60\t  sessionId: timestamp: number  // unix ms\n67\t}\n68\t\n69\t// UnstuckEvent — session progressed and is no longer stuck\n70\t{\n71\t  type: \"unstuck\"\n72\t  sessionId: string\n73\t  timestamp: number\n74\t}\n75\t\n76\t// SessionRegistered — initial session registration\n77\t{\n78\t  type: \"registered\"\n79\t  sessionId: string\n80\t  paneId: string\n81\t  cwd: string\n82\t  transcriptPath: string\n83\t  timestamp: number\n84\t}\n85\t\n86\t// SessionEnded — session terminated\n87\t{\n88\t  type: \"ended\"\n89\t  sessionId: string\n90\t  timestamp: number\n91\t}\n92\t```\n93\t\n94\t**How tmux detector submits events:**\n95\t\n96\tThe tmux detector (`daemon/tmux-adapter.ts`) emits normalized events to the daemon:\n97\t\n98\t- **Endpoint:** `POST \"stuck\";\n124\t}\n125\tfunction isUnstuckEvent(event): event is UnstuckEvent {\n126\t  return event?.type === \"unstuck\";\n127\t}\n128\tfunction isSessionRegistered(event): event is \"ended\";\n133\t}\n134\t```\n135\t\n136\t**Implementation status:** ✅ Complete\n137\t\n138\tThe `/event/normalized` endpoint is implemented in `daemon/index.ts` (lines 99-170) and handles all four event types. The Claude Code adapter (`daemon/claude-adapter.ts`) and tmux detector (`daemon/tmux-adapter.ts`) both emit normalized events to this endpoint.\n139\t\n140\t### Hooks, not polling\n141\t\n142\tDetection is event-driven via Claude Code hooks. A session emits a signal the moment control\n143\treturns to a human: while actively working it emits `PreToolUse`/`PostToolUse`, never `Stop`.\n144\tA session counts as waiting only once `Stop` or `PermissionRequest` has fired and no\n145\t`UserPromptSubmit` has come since. **Confirmed by probe (2026-05-25):** both `SessionStart` and\n146\t`Stop` fire in interactive and `-p` modes, the `Stop` payload carries `last_assistant_message`\n147\t(queue context for free), and hook commands inherit the ambient environment.\n148\t\n149\t### Stuck = needs attention, and stuck is stuck\n150\t\n151\tA session that has stopped or is waiting at a permission prompt cannot progress until the human\n152\tresponds — so it needs intervention by definition. Two collapses follow: there is no\n153\t\"finished but fine\" state (every stop is a queue item), and there is no permission-vs-stopped\n154\tpriority (it doesn't matter *why* it's stuck). `Stop` and `PermissionRequest` are both required\n155\tdetection triggers — a permission-blocked session is mid-turn and emits no `Stop` — but they're\n156\ttreated identically; `reason` is display-only and the queue is a flat FIFO dead-letter queue.\n157\t`Notification` is dropped (it adds nothing those two miss). The operator simply depletes the\n158\tqueue, and the next stuck session auto-loads.\n159\t\n160\t### Navigator, not relay (the delivery model)\n161\t\n162\tTrail Boss routes *attention*, it does not inject *input*. Sessions stay as long-running live\n163\tCLIs in tmux panes (Model A), and delivery happens by navigating the operator to the live pane\n164\t(`switch-client`/`select-window`/`select-pane`, optionally `link-window` to co-display) where\n165\tthey interact with the real prompt directly. This dissolves the send-keys fidelity problem,\n166\tmakes \"edit before allow\" native (you just type), and means no synthesized input ever reaches a\n167\tsession.\n168\t\n169\tRejected delivery alternatives:\n170\t\n171\t- **Resume-to-deliver** (`claude --resume <id>` in a second process): a live interactive CLI\n172\t  holds in-memory state and does not re-read its transcript, so a resumed process's reply never\n173\t  reaches the original pane; concurrent attach risks transcript divergence. `--fork-session`\n174\t  confirms plain `--resume` reuses the session. Only viable in a no-resident-process model\n175\t  (Model B), which we rejected for v1.\n176\t- **`send-keys` relay as the primary path:** retained only as a secondary plain-text option\n177\t  (basic submission confirmed working); native interaction is preferred.\n178\t- **`claude --remote-control`:** routes to the claude.ai / desktop / mobile surface, not a local\n179\t  channel — useless for a same-host tool.\n180\t- **Agent SDK `canUseTool` (Model B):** programmatic permission gating with `updatedInput` is\n181\t  attractive, but requires running sessions under the SDK instead of the terminal — deferred;\n182\t  the tmux-navigator model fits the existing workflow and the durability requirement.\n183\t\n184\t### Same-host daemon, durable via tmux\n185\t\n186\tTrail Boss does not need to live *inside* tmux to drive it — tmux is client/server, so any\n187\tsame-user process issues `tmux` commands to the server (pane ids are server-global). The\n188\tcontrol plane is an always-on daemon; presentation is transient (`display-popup` + keybinding).\n189\tBut for durability across SSH disconnect the daemon must survive SIGHUP, so it runs **in its own\n190\ttmux window** (simplest) or under **`systemd --user`** (also survives reboot; tmux does not).\n191\tAgents already persist because the tmux server is host-side. While disconnected, the daemon and\n192\thooks keep running, so the queue accumulates the backlog and disconnecting becomes a non-event.\n193\t\n194\t### The transcript is ground truth\n195\t\n196\tHooks are a low-latency notification; the transcript JSONL is authoritative. A reconcile loop\n197\tcorrects dropped hook POSTs, daemon restarts, and \"answered directly in the pane\" by checking\n198\twhether a session's transcript has advanced past its last `Stop`.\n199\t\n200\t## Tmux Detector Viability (2026-07-02)\n201\t\n202\t### Question\n203\tCan we build a purely tmux-level detector (no hooks) as a universal fallback for harnesses without hooks?\n204\t\n205\t### Verdict\n206\t**VIABLE — Works as designed**\n207\t\n208\tThe tmux detector (`daemon/tmux-detector.ts`) successfully implements harness-agnostic stuck detection through pane polling. It serves as a universal fallback for coding harnesses that lack hook support.\n209\t\n210\t### Implementation Status\n211\t- **Complete**: Fully implemented in TypeScript (Bun runtime)\n212\t- **Tested**: Acceptance scenario test exists (`test-tmux-detector.sh`)\n213\t- **Integrated**: Emits normalized events to daemon's `/event/normalized` endpoint\n214\t\n215\t### Reliability Assessment\n216\t\n217\t#### False Positive Rate: **Low**\n218\t**Mitigations applied:**\n219\t- **30-second quiet threshold** — avoids flagging momentary pauses (agent thinking, network latency)\n220\t- **Prompt pattern matching** — requires last line to match known prompt patterns (`$`, `>`, `#`, `?`, `[y/N]`, `:`, `>>>`, etc.)\n221\t- **Hash-based output comparison** — only flags stuck when pane content is genuinely unchanged\n222\t\n223\t**Result**: A pane must be quiet for 30+ seconds AND have a prompt-like last line to be considered stuck. This effectively eliminates false positives from active work.\n224\t\n225\t#### False Negative Rate: **User-dependent**\n226\t**Potential missed detections:**\n227\t- User forgets to set `@tb-` prefix on pane title → not monitored\n228\t- Session uses non-standard prompt pattern not in regex list → not detected as stuck\n229\t- Session produces output but is genuinely blocked (e.g., infinite loop with print statements)\n230\t\n231\t**Result**: False negatives are primarily due to opt-in compliance (user must remember `@tb-` prefix). This is acceptable for a fallback detector.\n232\t\n233\t#### Performance Impact: **Minimal**\n234\t**Metrics:**\n235\t- **Poll interval**: 2 seconds (configurable via `TRAILBOSS_POLL_INTERVAL_MS`)\n236\t- **Poll overhead**: `tmux capture-pane` is lightweight (text buffer copy)\n237\t- **CPU impact**: Negligible for <20 panes; acceptable for typical workloads\n238\t\n239\t**Measurement**: Each poll cycle runs `tmux list-panes -a` + one `capture-pane` per opted-in pane. On a system with 10 monitored panes, total execution time is <50ms per cycle.\n240\t\n241\t### Tuning Applied\n242\t\n243\t| Parameter | Default | Configurable via | Purpose |\n244\t|-----------|---------|------------------|---------|\n245\t| Quiet threshold | 30000ms (30s) | `TRAILBOSS_QUIET_THRESHOLD_MS` | Balance between speed and accuracy |\n246\t| Poll interval | 2000ms (2s) | `TRAILBOSS_POLL_INTERVAL_MS` | Detection latency vs CPU usage |\n247\t| Opt-in prefix | `@tb-` | `TRAILBOSS_OPT_IN_PREFIX` | Discoverable panes to monitor |\n248\t| Prompt patterns | 11 patterns | (code) | Reduce false positives |\n249\t\n250\t### How to Enable in Production\n251\t\n252\t**Option 1: Manual opt-in (recommended for testing)**\n253\t```bash\n254\t# In a tmux pane, set the title to opt-in\n255\ttmux rename-window '@tb-my-work'\n256\t\n257\t# Or set pane title\n258\ttmux select-pane -T '@tb-task-name'\n259\t```\n260\t\n261\t**Option 2: Run detector standalone**\n262\t```bash\n263\tcd /home/coding/trail-boss\n264\tbun run daemon/tmux-detector.ts\n265\t```\n266\t\n267\t**Option 3: Integrate with trailboss-start (future enhancement)**\n268\tAdd detector startup to `bin/trailboss-start` so it runs alongside the daemon:\n269\t```bash\n270\t# In trailboss-start, after starting daemon:\n271\tbun run daemon/tmux-detector.ts > ~/.local/share/trailboss/tmux-detector.log 2>&1 &\n272\t```\n273\t\n274\t### Limitations (Acceptable for Fallback)\n275\t\n276\t1. **No transcript path** — Synthetic sessions (`tmux-%446-timestamp`) have no `transcript.jsonl` to reconcile\n277\t2. **No permission vs stopped distinction** — Always emits `reason: \"stopped\"` (can't detect permission blocks without hooks)\n278\t3. **Opt-in required** — User must remember `@tb-` prefix\n279\t4. **Synthetic session IDs** — Not tied to harness session IDs; breaks across detector restarts\n280\t\n281\t### Comparison to Hook-Based Detection\n282\t\n283\t| Aspect | Hook-based (Claude Code) | Tmux detector (fallback) |\n284\t|--------|--------------------------|--------------------------|\n285\t| Fidelity | Full (session_id, transcript, cwd, reason) | Partial (synthetic session_id, no transcript, stopped-only) |\n286\t| Detection latency | Immediate (event-driven) | Delayed (30s quiet threshold) |\n287\t| False positives | None (exact state) | Low (prompt patterns + timeout) |\n288\t| Harness coupling | Claude Code only | Harness-agnostic |\n289\t| User action | None (automatic) | Opt-in required (set `@tb-` prefix) |\n290\t\n291\t### Conclusion\n292\t\n293\tThe tmux detector successfully answers Open question 1: **Yes, a purely tmux-level detector is viable as a universal fallback**. It provides harness-agnostic stuck detection with acceptable reliability and performance. For Claude Code sessions, hook-based detection remains primary (full fidelity, zero latency), but the detector enables Trail Boss to work with any future coding harness that lacks hooks.\n294\t\n295\tThe adapter seam is validated: the daemon consumes normalized events from either source (hooks or detector) without distinction. Switching remains tmux-level and harness-agnostic.\n296\t\n297\t## Test Results (2026-07-02)\n298\t\n299\t**Source:** Bead `tb-1me` — Tmux Detector Acceptance Test\n300\t\n301\t### Test Methodology\n302\t\n303\t**Acceptance Test**: Phase 7 Tmux Detector Acceptance Test (`test-tmux-detector.sh`)\n304\t\n305\t**Test Scenario**: harness-agnostic auto-discovery detector\n306\t- Creates isolated tmux server and test pane with `@tb-` prefix\n307\t- Verifies detector discovers pane via auto-discovery\n308\t- Waits for detector to flag pane as stuck (30s quiet threshold)\n309\t- Simulates activity in pane to trigger unstuck detection\n310\t- Verifies session is dequeued when activity resumes\n311\t\n312\t**Iterations**: 5 consecutive runs to measure consistency and detect flaky behavior\n313\t\n314\t**Environment**: Isolated tmux server per run (no shared state)\n315\t\n316\t### Execution Time Metrics\n317\t\n318\t| Metric | Value | Notes |\n319\t|--------|-------|-------|\n320\t| Total runs | 5 | Consecutive test iterations |\n321\t| Pass rate | 0% | All runs failed on test verification |\n322\t| Fail rate | 100% | Consistent failure mode |\n323\t| Average duration | 55.2s | Includes setup, test, cleanup |\n324\t| Median duration | 55.0s | Consistent execution time |\n325\t| Min duration | 54s | Fastest run |\n326\t| Max duration | 56s | Slowest run |\n327\t| Std deviation | 0.84s | Very low variance — stable execution |\n328\t\n329\t**Interpretation**: The 0.84s standard deviation across 5 runs indicates highly consistent execution time. The product runs a *herd* of\nagent sessions; when one gets stuck it reports in, and you — the trail boss — ride over and set\nit right. The metaphor maps cleanly onto the mechanism:\n\n- **the herd grazing the range** → sessions working autonomously\n- **a steer bogs down or strays** → a `Stop` / `PermissionRequest` hook fires; the collector\n  flags the session stuck\n- **the trail boss rides over and sets it right** → you read the context and give the order\n  (reply) or wave it on (skip); the queue surfaces stuck sessions oldest-first (flat FIFO, no\n  priority ranking)\n\n### Names considered and rejected\n\n- **`agent-inbox`** — clearest literal description, but collides head-on with\n  [`langchain-ai/agent-inbox`](https://github.com/langchain-ai/agent-inbox), an existing\n  human-in-the-loop inbox for LangGraph agents. Would read as derivative and lose every search.\n- **`agent-attention`** — names the value prop (your attention is the scarce resource being\n  routed), but risks reading as the ML \"attention\" mechanism.\n- **`agent-central`** — self-explanatory but generic, and \"central\" reads like a passive\n  dashboard/hub rather than an act-on-the-stuck-one tool.\n\nTrail Boss keeps a memorable, distinctive identity; the tagline carries the legibility for\nnewcomers.\n\n## Design decisions\n\n### Normalized event API endpoint (2026-07-02)\n\n**Decision:** Add a dedicated `/event/normalized` endpoint that accepts pre-normalized stuck/unstuck events.\n\n**Rationale:**\n\nThe daemon architecture separates detection (harness-coupled) from the core queue logic (harness-agnostic). To maintain this separation, we need a normalized event contract that isolates harness coupling to the adapter layer.\n\nTwo approaches were considered:\n\n1. **New normalized endpoint** (`/event/normalized`): Accepts pre-normalized events with a `type` field. Harness-specific adapters (Claude Code hooks, tmux detector) emit normalized events directly.\n2. **Server-side adapter wrapper**: Keep single `/event` endpoint, register multiple server-side adapters that wrap different event formats in a common Claude hook format.\n\n**Option 1 was chosen** for these reasons:\n\n- **Clean separation**: The adapter lives at the emission site (hook script or detector), not in the daemon. The daemon consumes only normalized events and has no knowledge of harness-specific formats.\n- **Protocol simplicity**: A single `type` field enables discriminated unions and type guards. No header-based routing or format detection required.\n- **Extensibility**: Adding a new harness means writing a new emitter/adapter that outputs normalized events; the daemon remains unchanged.\n- **Testability**: Synthetic events can be POSTed directly to `/event/normalized` without constructing hook payloads.\n\n**Event schema:**\n\nAll normalized events share a common structure with a `type` discriminator:\n\n```typescript\n// StuckEvent — session became stuck and needs attention\n{\n  type: \"stuck\"\n  sessionId: string\n  paneId: string\n  cwd: string\n  transcriptPath: string\n  reason: \"stopped\" | \"permission\"\n  message: string  // last_assistant_message or tool_name+input\n  timestamp: number  // unix ms\n}\n\n// UnstuckEvent — session progressed and is no longer stuck\n{\n  type: \"unstuck\"\n  sessionId: string\n  timestamp: number\n}\n\n// SessionRegistered — initial session registration\n{\n  type: \"registered\"\n  sessionId: string\n  paneId: string\n  cwd: string\n  transcriptPath: string\n  timestamp: number\n}\n\n// SessionEnded — session terminated\n{\n  type: \"ended\"\n  sessionId: string\n  timestamp: number\n}\n```\n\n**How tmux detector submits events:**\n\nThe tmux detector (`daemon/tmux-adapter.ts`) emits normalized events to the daemon:\n\n- **Endpoint:** `POST http://127.0.0.1:4000/event/normalized`\n- **Content-Type:** `application/json`\n- **Payload:** Normalized event JSON (see schema above)\n\nExample stuck event from tmux detector:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"type\": \"stuck\",\n  \"sessionId\": \"tmux-%446\",\n  \"paneId\": \"%446\",\n  \"cwd\": \"/home/coding/trail-boss\",\n  \"transcriptPath\": \"\",\n  \"reason\": \"stopped\",\n  \"message\": \"Quiet at prompt: $ \",\n  \"timestamp\": 1735689600000\n}\n```\n\n**Type guards:**\n\nThe daemon uses type guards based on the `type` field:\n\n```typescript\nfunction isStuckEvent(event): event is StuckEvent {\n  return event?.type === \"stuck\";\n}\nfunction isUnstuckEvent(event): event is UnstuckEvent {\n  return event?.type === \"unstuck\";\n}\nfunction isSessionRegistered(event): event is SessionRegistered {\n  return event?.type === \"registered\";\n}\nfunction isSessionEnded(event): event is SessionEnded {\n  return event?.type === \"ended\";\n}\n```\n\n**Implementation status:** ✅ Complete\n\nThe `/event/normalized` endpoint is implemented in `daemon/index.ts` (lines 99-170) and handles all four event types. The Claude Code adapter (`daemon/claude-adapter.ts`) and tmux detector (`daemon/tmux-adapter.ts`) both emit normalized events to this endpoint.\n\n### Hooks, not polling\n\nDetection is event-driven via Claude Code hooks. A session emits a signal the moment control\nreturns to a human: while actively working it emits `PreToolUse`/`PostToolUse`, never `Stop`.\nA session counts as waiting only once `Stop` or `PermissionRequest` has fired and no\n`UserPromptSubmit` has come since. **Confirmed by probe (2026-05-25):** both `SessionStart` and\n`Stop` fire in interactive and `-p` modes, the `Stop` payload carries `last_assistant_message`\n(queue context for free), and hook commands inherit the ambient environment.\n\n### Stuck = needs attention, and stuck is stuck\n\nA session that has stopped or is waiting at a permission prompt cannot progress until the human\nresponds — so it needs intervention by definition. Two collapses follow: there is no\n\"finished but fine\" state (every stop is a queue item), and there is no permission-vs-stopped\npriority (it doesn't matter *why* it's stuck). `Stop` and `PermissionRequest` are both required\ndetection triggers — a permission-blocked session is mid-turn and emits no `Stop` — but they're\ntreated identically; `reason` is display-only and the queue is a flat FIFO dead-letter queue.\n`Notification` is dropped (it adds nothing those two miss). The operator simply depletes the\nqueue, and the next stuck session auto-loads.\n\n### Navigator, not relay (the delivery model)\n\nTrail Boss routes *attention*, it does not inject *input*. Sessions stay as long-running live\nCLIs in tmux panes (Model A), and delivery happens by navigating the operator to the live pane\n(`switch-client`/`select-window`/`select-pane`, optionally `link-window` to co-display) where\nthey interact with the real prompt directly. This dissolves the send-keys fidelity problem,\nmakes \"edit before allow\" native (you just type), and means no synthesized input ever reaches a\nsession.\n\nRejected delivery alternatives:\n\n- **Resume-to-deliver** (`claude --resume <id>` in a second process): a live interactive CLI\n  holds in-memory state and does not re-read its transcript, so a resumed process's reply never\n  reaches the original pane; concurrent attach risks transcript divergence. `--fork-session`\n  confirms plain `--resume` reuses the session. Only viable in a no-resident-process model\n  (Model B), which we rejected for v1.\n- **`send-keys` relay as the primary path:** retained only as a secondary plain-text option\n  (basic submission confirmed working); native interaction is preferred.\n- **`claude --remote-control`:** routes to the claude.ai / desktop / mobile surface, not a local\n  channel — useless for a same-host tool.\n- **Agent SDK `canUseTool` (Model B):** programmatic permission gating with `updatedInput` is\n  attractive, but requires running sessions under the SDK instead of the terminal — deferred;\n  the tmux-navigator model fits the existing workflow and the durability requirement.\n\n### Same-host daemon, durable via tmux\n\nTrail Boss does not need to live *inside* tmux to drive it — tmux is client/server, so any\nsame-user process issues `tmux` commands to the server (pane ids are server-global). The\ncontrol plane is an always-on daemon; presentation is transient (`display-popup` + keybinding).\nBut for durability across SSH disconnect the daemon must survive SIGHUP, so it runs **in its own\ntmux window** (simplest) or under **`systemd --user`** (also survives reboot; tmux does not).\nAgents already persist because the tmux server is host-side. While disconnected, the daemon and\nhooks keep running, so the queue accumulates the backlog and disconnecting becomes a non-event.\n\n### The transcript is ground truth\n\nHooks are a low-latency notification; the transcript JSONL is authoritative. A reconcile loop\ncorrects dropped hook POSTs, daemon restarts, and \"answered directly in the pane\" by checking\nwhether a session's transcript has advanced past its last `Stop`.\n\n## Tmux Detector Viability (2026-07-02)\n\n### Question\nCan we build a purely tmux-level detector (no hooks) as a universal fallback for harnesses without hooks?\n\n### Verdict\n**VIABLE — Works as designed**\n\nThe tmux detector (`daemon/tmux-detector.ts`) successfully implements harness-agnostic stuck detection through pane polling. It serves as a universal fallback for coding harnesses that lack hook support.\n\n### Implementation Status\n- **Complete**: Fully implemented in TypeScript (Bun runtime)\n- **Tested**: Acceptance scenario test exists (`test-tmux-detector.sh`)\n- **Integrated**: Emits normalized events to daemon's `/event/normalized` endpoint\n\n### Reliability Assessment\n\n#### False Positive Rate: **Low**\n**Mitigations applied:**\n- **30-second quiet threshold** — avoids flagging momentary pauses (agent thinking, network latency)\n- **Prompt pattern matching** — requires last line to match known prompt patterns (`$`, `>`, `#`, `?`, `[y/N]`, `:`, `>>>`, etc.)\n- **Hash-based output comparison** — only flags stuck when pane content is genuinely unchanged\n\n**Result**: A pane must be quiet for 30+ seconds AND have a prompt-like last line to be considered stuck. This effectively eliminates false positives from active work.\n\n#### False Negative Rate: **User-dependent**\n**Potential missed detections:**\n- User forgets to set `@tb-` prefix on pane title → not monitored\n- Session uses non-standard prompt pattern not in regex list → not detected as stuck\n- Session produces output but is genuinely blocked (e.g., infinite loop with print statements)\n\n**Result**: False negatives are primarily due to opt-in compliance (user must remember `@tb-` prefix). This is acceptable for a fallback detector.\n\n#### Performance Impact: **Minimal**\n**Metrics:**\n- **Poll interval**: 2 seconds (configurable via `TRAILBOSS_POLL_INTERVAL_MS`)\n- **Poll overhead**: `tmux capture-pane` is lightweight (text buffer copy)\n- **CPU impact**: Negligible for <20 panes; acceptable for typical workloads\n\n**Measurement**: Each poll cycle runs `tmux list-panes -a` + one `capture-pane` per opted-in pane. On a system with 10 monitored panes, total execution time is <50ms per cycle.\n\n### Tuning Applied\n\n| Parameter | Default | Configurable via | Purpose |\n|-----------|---------|------------------|---------|\n| Quiet threshold | 30000ms (30s) | `TRAILBOSS_QUIET_THRESHOLD_MS` | Balance between speed and accuracy |\n| Poll interval | 2000ms (2s) | `TRAILBOSS_POLL_INTERVAL_MS` | Detection latency vs CPU usage |\n| Opt-in prefix | `@tb-` | `TRAILBOSS_OPT_IN_PREFIX` | Discoverable panes to monitor |\n| Prompt patterns | 11 patterns | (code) | Reduce false positives |\n\n### How to Enable in Production\n\n**Option 1: Manual opt-in (recommended for testing)**\n```bash\n# In a tmux pane, set the title to opt-in\ntmux rename-window '@tb-my-work'\n\n# Or set pane title\ntmux select-pane -T '@tb-task-name'\n```\n\n**Option 2: Run detector standalone**\n```bash\ncd /home/coding/trail-boss\nbun run daemon/tmux-detector.ts\n```\n\n**Option 3: Integrate with trailboss-start (future enhancement)**\nAdd detector startup to `bin/trailboss-start` so it runs alongside the daemon:\n```bash\n# In trailboss-start, after starting daemon:\nbun run daemon/tmux-detector.ts > ~/.local/share/trailboss/tmux-detector.log 2>&1 &\n```\n\n### Limitations (Acceptable for Fallback)\n\n1. **No transcript path** — Synthetic sessions (`tmux-%446-timestamp`) have no `transcript.jsonl` to reconcile\n2. **No permission vs stopped distinction** — Always emits `reason: \"stopped\"` (can't detect permission blocks without hooks)\n3. **Opt-in required** — User must remember `@tb-` prefix\n4. **Synthetic session IDs** — Not tied to harness session IDs; breaks across detector restarts\n\n### Comparison to Hook-Based Detection\n\n| Aspect | Hook-based (Claude Code) | Tmux detector (fallback) |\n|--------|--------------------------|--------------------------|\n| Fidelity | Full (session_id, transcript, cwd, reason) | Partial (synthetic session_id, no transcript, stopped-only) |\n| Detection latency | Immediate (event-driven) | Delayed (30s quiet threshold) |\n| False positives | None (exact state) | Low (prompt patterns + timeout) |\n| Harness coupling | Claude Code only | Harness-agnostic |\n| User action | None (automatic) | Opt-in required (set `@tb-` prefix) |\n\n### Conclusion\n\nThe tmux detector successfully answers Open question 1: **Yes, a purely tmux-level detector is viable as a universal fallback**. It provides harness-agnostic stuck detection with acceptable reliability and performance. For Claude Code sessions, hook-based detection remains primary (full fidelity, zero latency), but the detector enables Trail Boss to work with any future coding harness that lacks hooks.\n\nThe adapter seam is validated: the daemon consumes normalized events from either source (hooks or detector) without distinction. Switching remains tmux-level and harness-agnostic.\n\n## Test Results (2026-07-02)\n\n**Source:** Bead `tb-1me` — Tmux Detector Acceptance Test\n\n### Test Methodology\n\n**Acceptance Test**: Phase 7 Tmux Detector Acceptance Test (`test-tmux-detector.sh`)\n\n**Test Scenario**: harness-agnostic auto-discovery detector\n- Creates isolated tmux server and test pane with `@tb-` prefix\n- Verifies detector discovers pane via auto-discovery\n- Waits for detector to flag pane as stuck (30s quiet threshold)\n- Simulates activity in pane to trigger unstuck detection\n- Verifies session is dequeued when activity resumes\n\n**Iterations**: 5 consecutive runs to measure consistency and detect flaky behavior\n\n**Environment**: Isolated tmux server per run (no shared state)\n\n### Execution Time Metrics\n\n| Metric | Value | Notes |\n|--------|-------|-------|\n| Total runs | 5 | Consecutive test iterations |\n| Pass rate | 0% | All runs failed on test verification |\n| Fail rate | 100% | Consistent failure mode |\n| Average duration | 55.2s | Includes setup, test, cleanup |\n| Median duration | 55.0s | Consistent execution time |\n| Min duration | 54s | Fastest run |\n| Max duration | 56s | Slowest run |\n| Std deviation | 0.84s | Very low variance — stable execution |\n\n**Interpretation**: The 0.84s standard deviation across 5 runs indicates highly consistent execution time. Test verification failed because it expected pane `%0` but found `%22`\n\n**Evidence from logs**:\n1. Pane correctly detected as stuck after ~21-27s (✓)\n2. Detector logs show both panes being discovered and tracked\n\n**This is a test infrastructure issue, not a detector bug**: The detector is designed to discover opted-in panes across all tmux servers on the system. This is the correct behavior for production use (you want to monitor your coding sessions regardless of which tmux server they're in). The test needs better isolation.\n\n### Flaky Behavior Assessment\n\n**Consistency**: **High** — All 5 runs failed identically with same failure type and duration range (54-56s)\n\n**Flakiness**: **None detected** — The consistent failure mode points to a systematic test infrastructure issue rather than intermittent detector behavior. The detector itself performs consistently across all runs.\n\n### Conclusions\n\n1. **Detector core functionality is working correctly**:\n   - Auto-discovery of `@tb-` prefixed panes: ✓\n   - Stuck detection after 30s quiet threshold: ✓\n   - Queue entry creation: ✓\n   - Multi-server discovery works as designed ✓\n\n2. **Test infrastructure has an isolation issue**:\n   - Detector correctly discovers opted-in panes across ALL tmux servers\n   - Test isolation only covers the test server, not the main tmux server\n   - This is a test-only issue — in production, multi-server discovery is the desired behavior\n   - The detector is working correctly; the test needs better isolation\n\n3. **Performance meets requirements**:\n   - Sub-second detection latency once quiet threshold is reached\n   - Minimal CPU overhead (2s poll interval, lightweight tmux commands)\n   - Consistent execution time with low variance\n\n4. **No false positives/negatives in core detection**:\n   - The detector correctly distinguishes between active and stuck states\n   - Prompt pattern matching effectively filters momentary pauses\n   - Hash-based comparison prevents false positives from unchanged output\n\n### Recommendations\n\n1. **For production deployment**: The detector is ready. Each session periodically stalls waiting on **you**: a permission prompt,\n14\ta clarifying question, or a finished turn awaiting the next instruction. Today you find those\n15\tstalls by **manually cycling windows**. That polling is the bottleneck: most of your time goes\n16\tto *finding* the session that needs you, not *answering* it, and blocked sessions burn\n17\twall-clock while otherwise-parallel work waits.\n18\t\n19\t---\n20\t\n21\t## Operating principles\n22\t\n23\t### Human *on* the loop, not *in* it\n24\t\n25\tClassic agentic HITL wires you into the inner cycle — approving each step, answering each\n26\tprompt — so you are the bottleneck on every iteration. Trail Boss flips it: agents run\n27\tautonomously by default and you supervise from above, **engaged only by exception**. When an\n28\tagent can't proceed on its own, it falls through to you.\n29\t\n30\t**The human is the failure mode.** Trail Boss is a **dead-letter queue for a fleet of agents**:\n31\tthe happy path never touches you; only stalled work routes to you, you process the exception\n32\t(reply or skip), and it goes back on the wire.\n33\t\n34\t### The \"stuck = needs attention\" axiom — and stuck is stuck\n35\t\n36\tA session that has stopped *or* is waiting at a permission prompt cannot progress toward its\n37\tgoal until the human responds — therefore it needs intervention, by definition. This collapses\n38\ttwo fuzzy questions at once:\n39\t\n40\t- **No \"idle vs. done\" distinction.** There is no separate \"finished but fine\" state; if it\n41\t  stopped and you haven't responded, it's waiting on you. Every stop is a queue item.\n42\t- **No \"permission vs. stopped\" distinction.** It doesn't matter *why* a session is stuck —\n43\t  both mean \"blocked until the human acts.\" The two are detected by different hooks (see below)\n44\t  but are **treated identically** in the queue. `reason` is display-only metadata, never a\n45\t  priority input.\n46\t\n47\tSo the queue is a flat **dead-letter queue**: stuck sessions accumulate and the operator\n48\tdepletes them. (The deeper fix — making the interactive CLIs longer-running so they stop less\n49\toften — is a separate workstream, not Trail Boss's concern.)\n50\t\n51\t### Navigator, not relay\n52\t\n53\tTrail Boss does **not** inject answers into sessions. It routes *your attention* to the live\n54\tsession and you interact with the real CLI directly. It is an attention router + tmux\n55\tnavigator, not an input relay or an autonomous responder. (Rationale and the rejected\n56\talternatives are in [`../notes/decisions.md`](../notes/decisions.md).)\n57\t\n58\t---\n59\t\n60\t## Non-goals\n61\t\n62\t- **Not a fleet spawner / supervisor.** Trail Boss does not launch, kill, or cost-optimize\n63\t  agents. It assumes sessions already exist and surfaces the stuck ones. (Spawning is the job\n64\t  of separate fleet tooling.)\n65\t- **Not an autonomous responder.** It never synthesizes or auto-sends a reply. It only routes\n66\t  you to a session; all input is human-authored, typed into the real CLI.\n67\t- **Not multi-operator / multi-tenant.** Single operator, single host, single tmux server.\n68\t- **Not a remote web product.** It is a same-host, tmux-native tool whose sole job is to\n69\t  eliminate manual tab-switching. Remote access is out of scope for v1.\n70\t- **Not dependent on plan mode.** Vanilla Claude Code plan mode is assumed disabled (the\n71\t  operator uses their own); the `reason` enum is exactly two values — **`permission`** and\n72\t  **`stopped`**.\n73\t\n74\t---\n75\t\n76\t## Session & delivery model\n77\t\n78\tThere are two mutually exclusive ways to run agent sessions; Trail Boss commits to one.\n79\t\n80\t- **Model A — live panes (CHOSEN).** Long-running interactive CLIs stay resident in tmux\n81\t  panes. Delivery happens by *interacting with the live process* — Trail Boss navigates you to\n82\t  it. Survives disconnect via tmux (see Architecture).\n83\t- **Model B — transcript sessions (rejected for v1).** No resident process; a session exists\n84\t  only as its transcript, and a fresh `claude --resume <id>` is spawned per turn with Trail\n85\t  Boss rendering output itself.\n86\t\n87\t**Why not Model B / resume-to-deliver:** a session's durable state is its transcript JSONL, but\n88\ta *live* interactive CLI holds its own in-memory copy and does not re-read that file for\n89\toutside changes. Running a second `claude --resume <id>` while the original is alive yields two\n90\tprocesses over one transcript: the resuming process produces the response *in itself*, the\n91\toriginal pane never reflects it, and concurrent writes risk divergence. The existence of\n92\t`--fork-session` (\"create a new session ID instead of reusing the original\") confirms plain\n93\t`--resume` reuses the session and is not designed for a concurrent second attach. So a reply\n94\tdelivered via resume **does not** reach the original interactive pane. Model A + direct\n95\tinteraction sidesteps this entirely.\n96\t\n97\t---\n98\t\n99\t## What is needed (capabilities)\n100\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"6b9d79bc-5d0c-4a69-9749-3d3a808fc070","uuid":"3c14d4c9-a57a-4191-8a5b-d452a99e1833","timestamp":"2026-07-03T02:25:26.772Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"/home/coding/trail-boss/docs/plan/plan.md","content":"# Trail Boss — design plan\n\nThe complete design: the problem, operating principles, the session/delivery model, the\narchitecture, what's been empirically confirmed, the phases, and the open questions. See\n[`../research/claude-code-mechanics.md`](../research/claude-code-mechanics.md) for the Claude\nCode primitives and [`../research/related-work.md`](../research/related-work.md) for prior art.\n\n---\n\n## Problem\n\nYou run long-form, human-in-the-loop agentic coding across many concurrent agent sessions,\none per tmux window. Each session periodically stalls waiting on **you**: a permission prompt,\na clarifying question, or a finished turn awaiting the next instruction. Today you find those\nstalls by **manually cycling windows**. That polling is the bottleneck: most of your time goes\nto *finding* the session that needs you, not *answering* it, and blocked sessions burn\nwall-clock while otherwise-parallel work waits.\n\n---\n\n## Operating principles\n\n### Human *on* the loop, not *in* it\n\nClassic agentic HITL wires you into the inner cycle — approving each step, answering each\nprompt — so you are the bottleneck on every iteration. Trail Boss flips it: agents run\nautonomously by default and you supervise from above, **engaged only by exception**. When an\nagent can't proceed on its own, it falls through to you.\n\n**The human is the failure mode.** Trail Boss is a **dead-letter queue for a fleet of agents**:\nthe happy path never touches you; only stalled work routes to you, you process the exception\n(reply or skip), and it goes back on the wire.\n\n### The \"stuck = needs attention\" axiom — and stuck is stuck\n\nA session that has stopped *or* is waiting at a permission prompt cannot progress toward its\ngoal until the human responds — therefore it needs intervention, by definition. This collapses\ntwo fuzzy questions at once:\n\n- **No \"idle vs. done\" distinction.** There is no separate \"finished but fine\" state; if it\n  stopped and you haven't responded, it's waiting on you. Every stop is a queue item.\n- **No \"permission vs. stopped\" distinction.** It doesn't matter *why* a session is stuck —\n  both mean \"blocked until the human acts.\" The two are detected by different hooks (see below)\n  but are **treated identically** in the queue. `reason` is display-only metadata, never a\n  priority input.\n\nSo the queue is a flat **dead-letter queue**: stuck sessions accumulate and the operator\ndepletes them. (The deeper fix — making the interactive CLIs longer-running so they stop less\noften — is a separate workstream, not Trail Boss's concern.)\n\n### Navigator, not relay\n\nTrail Boss does **not** inject answers into sessions. It routes *your attention* to the live\nsession and you interact with the real CLI directly. It is an attention router + tmux\nnavigator, not an input relay or an autonomous responder. (Rationale and the rejected\nalternatives are in [`../notes/decisions.md`](../notes/decisions.md).)\n\n---\n\n## Non-goals\n\n- **Not a fleet spawner / supervisor.** Trail Boss does not launch, kill, or cost-optimize\n  agents. It assumes sessions already exist and surfaces the stuck ones. (Spawning is the job\n  of separate fleet tooling.)\n- **Not an autonomous responder.** It never synthesizes or auto-sends a reply. It only routes\n  you to a session; all input is human-authored, typed into the real CLI.\n- **Not multi-operator / multi-tenant.** Single operator, single host, single tmux server.\n- **Not a remote web product.** It is a same-host, tmux-native tool whose sole job is to\n  eliminate manual tab-switching. Remote access is out of scope for v1.\n- **Not dependent on plan mode.** Vanilla Claude Code plan mode is assumed disabled (the\n  operator uses their own); the `reason` enum is exactly two values — **`permission`** and\n  **`stopped`**.\n\n---\n\n## Session & delivery model\n\nThere are two mutually exclusive ways to run agent sessions; Trail Boss commits to one.\n\n- **Model A — live panes (CHOSEN).** Long-running interactive CLIs stay resident in tmux\n  panes. Delivery happens by *interacting with the live process* — Trail Boss navigates you to\n  it. Survives disconnect via tmux (see Architecture).\n- **Model B — transcript sessions (rejected for v1).** No resident process; a session exists\n  only as its transcript, and a fresh `claude --resume <id>` is spawned per turn with Trail\n  Boss rendering output itself.\n\n**Why not Model B / resume-to-deliver:** a session's durable state is its transcript JSONL, but\na *live* interactive CLI holds its own in-memory copy and does not re-read that file for\noutside changes. Running a second `claude --resume <id>` while the original is alive yields two\nprocesses over one transcript: the resuming process produces the response *in itself*, the\noriginal pane never reflects it, and concurrent writes risk divergence. The existence of\n`--fork-session` (\"create a new session ID instead of reusing the original\") confirms plain\n`--resume` reuses the session and is not designed for a concurrent second attach. So a reply\ndelivered via resume **does not** reach the original interactive pane. Model A + direct\ninteraction sidesteps this entirely.\n\n---\n\n## What is needed (capabilities)\n","numLines":100,"startLine":1,"totalLines":765}}}

Raw Claude Hook Payload Structure\n\nThe raw `HookEvent` from Claude Code hooks (defined in `daemon/types.ts`):\n\n```typescript\ninterface HookEvent {\n  session_id: string;\n  transcript_path: string;\n  cwd: string;\n  hook_event_name: \"Stop\" | \"PermissionRequest\" | \"UserPromptSubmit\" | \"SessionStart\" | \"SessionEnd\";\n  permission_mode?: string;\n  effort?: { level: string };\n  // Stop-specific\n  last_assistant_message?: string;\n  stop_hook_active?: boolean;\n  background_tasks?: string[];\n  session_crons?: string[];\n  // PermissionRequest-specific\n  tool_name?: string;\n  tool_input?: unknown;\n  permission_suggestions?: Array<{ type: string; mode: string; destination: string }>;\n}\n```\n\n**Key characteristics:**\n- Harness-coupled (Claude Code-specific)\n- Has optional fields per event type\n- No `type` discriminator — uses `hook_event_name` string enum\n- Carries rich metadata (effort, background_tasks, etc.) not needed by queue\n\n---\n\n## 2.
